lead: Laminated object manufacturing (LOM) glues thin sheets one on another and cuts each sheet to the cross-section shape. A heated roller bonds the sheet; a laser or blade cuts the outline; the platform drops by one sheet thickness. Sheet is cheap and the leftover block holds the part, so large models need no extra support. It is used for big concept models, casting patterns and paper or plastic prototypes.
prereq: You need: Chapter 7.2 for the CAD-to-part chain and slicing, and Unit 3, Sheet Metal and Plastics Processing, for handling thin sheets.

blocks.text: LOM is a sheet lamination process. The raw material is a thin sheet, not powder, filament or liquid. The sheet is bonded to the layer below, cut to the outline, and a fresh sheet is laid on top. The part is a stack of glued sheets. Sheet thickness t is fixed by the roll, usually 0.05 mm to 0.2 mm; 0.1 mm paper is common.

The machine has a supply roll for fresh sheet, a take-up roll for spent sheet, a heated roller that presses the sheet and activates adhesive, and a cutting head (laser or blade) that traces the cross-section. The platform drops one sheet thickness after each layer so the stack top stays at the cutter focus.

Most LOM sheet is paper coated on one side with heat-activated adhesive, so no glue is spread at the machine. Plastic sheet, metal foil and ceramic green tape are also used. Sheet is cheap per square metre, making LOM a low-cost route for large parts. No separate support is needed: unused sheet stays in place and holds every overhang.

head: Feature
Typical LOM value
rows: t + glue line; about 0.1 mm for 0.1 mm paper
laser for paper, blade for some tapes
break out waste, sand, seal or paint

blocks.where: n is the number of layers (no unit); H is the part height in mm; t is the sheet thickness in mm.

items: The CAD model is sliced into layers of thickness t, equal to the sheet thickness.
The platform sits at the top of its stroke. The supply roll feeds one sheet over the previous layer.
The heated roller presses down. Heat softens the adhesive and the new sheet bonds to the layer below.
The cutting head traces the outline of this layer's cross-section. On paper machines the laser also cuts a grid outside the part.
The platform moves down by t, bringing the stack top back to the cutter's focal plane.
The take-up roll winds the spent sheet and the next sheet is fed. Steps 2 to 5 repeat for all n layers.
The block is taken out, the grid-cut waste is broken away, and the part is sanded, sealed or painted.

blocks.where: T is the build time in s; n is the number of layers; t<sub>b</sub> is the time to feed and bond one sheet in s; t<sub>c</sub> is the time to cut one layer in s.

blocks.text: Bonding is a whole-sheet roller pass, not point by point. So a tall part with a large footprint builds fast; LOM suits big block-like models more than small detailed ones.

Outside the part outline the laser cuts a square grid, the cross-hatch, breaking the surrounding block into small cubes. After the build the operator lifts out the block and snaps the cubes off by hand or knife: de-cubing. The part leaves with stepped walls and slightly frayed edges, so sanding, sealing or painting follows. The excess is the same sheet cut loose, not a separate support.

In-plane accuracy (X–Y outline) depends on beam or blade position and is about ±0.1 mm to ±0.2 mm. Z depends on the sheet: each layer is one sheet plus one glue line, so vertical faces arrive in steps of t. A 0.1 mm sheet gives 0.1 mm steps. Thinner sheet gives smoother walls but more layers and build time.

items: Advantages: cheap sheet material, large parts, no separate supports, low shrinkage because the sheet is not melted, and no chemical post-curing; post-processing is simple in tools but labour-heavy because de-cubing is done by hand.
Limits: one sheet material per part, visible Z steps, delamination if paper is damp or the roller is cold, fragile thin walls, and waste trapped inside closed hollow shapes.

figure.caption: The sheet is glued, pressed and cut, then the platform drops one thickness and the cycle repeats. The cut alone sets the cross-section of each layer; breaking out the waste and finishing the part happen only once, after the whole stack is built.

examples.question: A 50 mm × 50 mm × 30 mm block is built by LOM from 0.1 mm paper. The machine uses one full 50 mm × 50 mm sheet per layer. Find (a) layers, (b) sheet area in m², (c) material cost at ₹40 per m².
steps: n = H ÷ t = 30 mm ÷ 0.1 mm = 300 layers.
One layer area A₁ = 50 mm × 50 mm = 2500 mm².
examples.answer: 300 layers, 0.75 m² of paper sheet, and a material cost of ₹30.
examples.check:
H = 30.0
t = 0.1
n = H / t
print(n)
L = 50.0
W = 50.0
A1 = L * W
A = n * A1
print(A)
A_m2 = A / 1e6
print(A_m2)
cost = A_m2 * 40
print(cost)

traps: LOM bonds and cuts sheets. It does not melt powder (powder bed fusion, Chapter 7.5) or cure resin (stereolithography, Chapter 7.3).
Z accuracy is set by sheet thickness and glue line, not laser spot size. A fine beam still gives steps of t.
The surrounding material is the same sheet, cut loose, not separate support. It must still be removed by de-cubing.
Layer count is H ÷ t. Do not divide volume by sheet area and lose the unit of t.

The glue line makes each bonded layer slightly thicker than t, so the stack is a little taller than n × t. To hit height H exactly, use n = H ÷ (t + glue line) — slightly fewer layers than H ÷ t — and sand the top face for the final allowance.

quiz.q: What holds an overhang in a LOM build?
quiz.a: The unused sheet block. The sheet bonds over the whole platform, so material beside the part supports it until de-cubing.

quiz.q: Name the two cutting methods used in LOM.
quiz.a: A focused laser beam for paper, and a mechanical blade or knife in some tape systems.

quiz.q: Why is the waste area cross-hatched before de-cubing?
quiz.a: The laser cuts a square grid into the surrounding sheet, breaking the solid block into small cubes. These snap off by hand without levering against the part and damaging thin walls.

quiz.q: Why does vertical accuracy depend on the sheet rather than the cutter?
quiz.a: The cutter shapes only the outline inside one layer. Layer height is fixed by sheet thickness plus adhesive line, so vertical faces are steps of that size.

quiz.q: A 20 mm tall part uses 0.08 mm sheet. Each layer takes 15 s to feed, bond and cut. Find layers and build time.
A 25 mm tall part with 80 mm × 60 mm footprint uses 0.125 mm sheet, one full footprint sheet per layer. Sheet costs ₹50 per m². Find layers and material cost.
A paper LOM part shows horizontal steps and one corner peels a week after build. Give likely causes and one remedy each.
quiz.a: Steps come from layer thickness: use thinner sheet, or sand and seal. Peeling means weak bonding: damp paper, dust, or a cold/lightly loaded roller. Store sheet dry, clean the roller, raise temperature and pressure, and seal the part against moisture.

quiz.q: Why is LOM a poor choice for a thin-walled closed hollow sphere?
quiz.a: Waste inside the hollow cannot be reached for de-cubing, so it stays trapped. The wall must be at least about one sheet thick, and thin curved walls are fragile while waste is broken away. Powder bed or resin processes leave loose material that pours out.

beyond: Not for the exam. Sheet lamination has moved past paper. Metal foil can be welded layer by layer by ultrasonic consolidation: a rolling sonotrode scrubs and bonds the foil, and a small milling tool restores the outline, so no adhesive or de-cubing is needed. That route embeds sensors, cooling channels and fibres inside solid metal parts, and is used for heat exchangers and tooling inserts. Ceramic green tape lamination builds stacked electronic substrates co-fired in one furnace. Search for ultrasonic additive manufacturing, tape casting and green tape lamination.
